# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0.149/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize JSON data to a Rust data structure.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- When serializing or deserializing JSON goes wrong.
- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- A map of String to serde_json::Value.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)- `std`
- Serialize a Rust data structure into JSON data.
- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)
- The Value enum, a loosely typed way of representing any valid JSON value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [json](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html)
- Construct a `serde_json::Value`from a JSON literal.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html)
- A structure that deserializes JSON into Rust values.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- This type represents all possible errors that can occur when serializing or deserializing JSON data.
- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- Represents a JSON key/value type.
- [Number](https://docs.rs/struct.Number.html)
- Represents a JSON number, whether integer or floating point.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html)- `std`
- A structure for serializing Rust values into JSON.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamDeserializer.html)- Deserializer
- Iterator that deserializes a stream into multiple JSON values.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)
- Represents any valid JSON value.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)- reader - `std`
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from an I/O stream of JSON.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)- slice
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from bytes of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html)- str
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from a string of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_value.html)- value
- Interpret a `serde_json::Value`as an instance of type`T`.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html)- string - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string_pretty.html)- string_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_value.html)- value
- Convert a `T`into`serde_json::Value`which is an enum that can represent any valid JSON data.
- [to_vec](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)- `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec_pretty.html)- vec_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)- writer - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as JSON into the I/O stream.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer_pretty.html)- writer_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as pretty-printed JSON into the I/O stream.

# numeris - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/numeris/0.5.14/target-redirect/numeris/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#numeris)numeris

Pure-Rust numerical algorithms library — high performance with SIMD support (NEON, SSE2, AVX, AVX-512) while also supporting no-std for embedded and WASM targets. Similar in scope to SciPy.

**Documentation & examples:** [https://numeris-rs.dev/](https://numeris-rs.dev/)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use numeris::{Matrix, Vector};
// Solve a linear system Ax = b
let a = Matrix::new([
    [2.0_f64, 1.0, -1.0],
    [-3.0, -1.0, 2.0],
    [-2.0, 1.0, 2.0],
]);
let b = Vector::from_array([8.0, -11.0, -3.0]);
let x = a.solve(&b).unwrap(); // x = [2, 3, -1]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

-
[ `matrix`] — Fixed-size`Matrix<T, M, N>`with const-generic dimensions. Stack-allocated`[[T; M]; N]`column-major storage (matches LAPACK conventions).`Matrix::new()`accepts row-major input and transposes internally. Includes arithmetic, indexing, norms, block operations, and iteration.`Vector<T, N>`
-
`dynmatrix``DynMatrix<T>`with runtime dimensions (requires`alloc`feature, included with`std`).`Vec<T>`column-major storage (`col * nrows + row`).`from_rows()`accepts row-major data (transposes internally);`from_slice()`accepts column-major data directly. Implements`MatrixRef``MatrixMut``DynVector<T>``DynLu`,`DynCholesky`,`DynQr`,`DynSvd`,`DynSymmetricEigen`,`DynSchur`wrapper structs.
-
`linalg``solve()`,`inverse()`,`det()`,`eigenvalues()`, etc. Free functions operate on`&mut impl MatrixMut<T>`for in-place use; wrapper structs offer a higher-level API. Convenience methods on both`Matrix`and`DynMatrix`.
-
`ode``ode`feature.
-
`optim``optim::brent``optim::newton_1d``optim::minimize_bfgs``optim::least_squares_gn``optim::least_squares_lm``optim::minimize_bfgs_dyn``optim::least_squares_gn_dyn``optim::least_squares_lm_dyn``optim::finite_difference_gradient_dyn``optim::finite_difference_jacobian_dyn``DynVector``DynMatrix``alloc`feature. Requires`optim`feature.
-
`control``control::Biquad``control::BiquadCascade``control::Pid``control::lead_compensator``control::lag_compensator``control::FopdtModel``control::ziegler_nichols_ultimate``complex`feature dependency. Requires`control`feature.
-
`estimate``estimate::Ekf``estimate::Ukf``estimate::SrUkf``estimate::Ckf``estimate::rts_smooth``estimate::BatchLsq``alloc`. Requires`estimate`feature.
-
`interp``interp::LinearInterp``interp::HermiteInterp``interp::LagrangeInterp``interp::CubicSpline``interp::BilinearInterp``Dyn*`, requires`alloc`). Out-of-bounds evaluations extrapolate. Requires`interp`feature.
-
`imageproc``DynMatrix`buffers. Full toolkit: convolution (`imageproc::convolve2d``imageproc::convolve2d_separable``DynMatrix<u32>`or row-major`Vec<u32>`labels image), geometric utilities (flip, rotate 90°/180°/270°, pad, crop, resize bilinear and nearest). See`imageproc``imageproc`feature (implies`alloc`).
-
`special``special::gamma``special::lgamma``special::digamma``special::beta``special::lbeta``special::gamma_inc``special::gamma_inc_upper``special::betainc``special::erf``special::erfc``FloatScalar`(f32/f64), fully no-std. Requires`special`feature.
-
`quad``quad::gauss_legendre``quad::adaptive_simpson``quad::trapezoid``quad::simpson``quad`feature.
-
`stats``stats::ContinuousDistribution``stats::DiscreteDistribution``stats::Normal``stats::Uniform``stats::Exponential``stats::Gamma``stats::Beta``stats::ChiSquared``stats::StudentT``stats::Bernoulli``stats::Binomial``stats::Poisson``stats::Rng``sample()`/`sample_array()`on every distribution. Requires`stats`feature (implies`special`).
-
`quaternion``[w, x, y, z]`. Construct from axis-angle, Euler angles, or rotation matrices. Supports Hamilton product, vector rotation, SLERP, and conversion back to matrices.
-
`traits`- `Scalar`- `Copy + PartialEq + Debug + Zero + One + Num`)
- `FloatScalar`- `Scalar + Float`), used by quaternions
- `LinalgScalar`
- `MatrixRef`- `MatrixMut`

[§](https://docs.rs#complex-matrices)Complex matrices

Enable the `complex` feature to use decompositions with `Complex<f32>` /
`Complex<f64>`. Cholesky generalizes to Hermitian (A = LL^H), QR uses
complex Householder reflections, and norms return real values. Zero overhead
for real-only code paths.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

| Feature | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `std` | yes | Implies `alloc`. Hardware FPU via system libm |
| `alloc` | via std | `DynMatrix`/`DynVector`(heap-allocated, runtime-sized) |
| `ode` | no | ODE integration (RK4, adaptive solvers) |
| `optim` | no | Optimization (root finding, BFGS, Gauss-Newton, LM) |
| `control` | no | Digital IIR filters, PID, lead/lag compensators, PID tuning |
| `estimate` | no | State estimation (EKF, UKF). Implies `alloc` |
| `interp` | no | Interpolation (linear, Hermite, Lagrange, cubic spline, bilinear 2D) |
| `imageproc` | no | 2D image processing: filters, morphology, integral image, thresholding, Canny, corners, DoG, pyramid, geometric. Implies `alloc` |
| `quad` | no | Numerical quadrature (Gauss-Legendre, adaptive Simpson, composite rules) |
| `special` | no | Special functions (gamma, beta, erf, incomplete gamma/beta) |
| `stats` | no | Statistical distributions (Normal, Gamma, etc.) with sampling. Implies `special` |
| `libm` | baseline | Pure-Rust software float fallback |
| `complex` | no | `Complex<f32>`/`Complex<f64>`support via`num-complex` |
| `nalgebra` | no | Conversions between numeris and nalgebra types |
| `serde` | no | Serialize/deserialize all types via serde |
| `rayon` | no | Multi-threaded parallelism on runtime-sized paths (e.g. dynamic finite-difference Jacobians, most `imageproc`filters). Implies`std` |
| `all` | no | All features |

[§](https://docs.rs#parallelism)Parallelism

SIMD is always-on and parallelizes *within* a core; the optional `rayon`
feature parallelizes *across* cores, and the two compose. It is opt-in
(rayon needs `std`, so it is never part of the no-std baseline) and purely
additive — builds without it are unchanged. Only heap-backed, runtime-sized
paths with independent, disjoint output columns are parallelized: dynamic
finite-difference Jacobians (the separate `_par` routines
[ optim::finite_difference_jacobian_dyn_par](https://docs.rs/optim/fn.finite_difference_jacobian_dyn_par.html),

[) and most](https://docs.rs/optim/fn.finite_difference_gradient_dyn_par.html)

`optim::finite_difference_gradient_dyn_par``imageproc` filters
(convolution/blur, rank & median, morphology, resize, local statistics).
Small fixed-size [operations and order-sensitive reductions are never parallelized. Each routine gates on total work (so small inputs stay sequential) and writes to disjoint slices, so results are identical regardless of thread count. Speedups run ~2.5–4× on large images.](https://docs.rs/matrix/struct.Matrix.html)

`Matrix`The feature is purely additive — it never changes an existing signature
(the parallel optim routines are *new* `_par` functions; the sequential ones
keep their `FnMut` bound).

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/numeris/0.5.14/src/numeris/lib.rs.html

# numeris/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # numeris
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! Pure-Rust numerical algorithms library — high performance with SIMD support
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! (NEON, SSE2, AVX, AVX-512) while also supporting no-std for embedded and WASM
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! targets. Similar in scope to SciPy.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! **Documentation & examples:** <https://numeris-rs.dev/>
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ## Quick start
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! ```
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! use numeris::{Matrix, Vector};
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! // Solve a linear system Ax = b
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! let a = Matrix::new([
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!     [2.0_f64, 1.0, -1.0],
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!     [-3.0, -1.0, 2.0],
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!     [-2.0, 1.0, 2.0],
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ]);
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! let b = Vector::from_array([8.0, -11.0, -3.0]);
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! let x = a.solve(&b).unwrap(); // x = [2, 3, -1]
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! ```
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ## Modules
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! - [`matrix`] — Fixed-size `Matrix<T, M, N>` with const-generic dimensions.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!   Stack-allocated `[[T; M]; N]` column-major storage (matches LAPACK conventions).
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!   `Matrix::new()` accepts row-major input and transposes internally.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!   Includes arithmetic, indexing, norms, block operations, and iteration.
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!   [`Vector<T, N>`] is a type alias for an N×1 column matrix (matching
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!   nalgebra convention).
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! - [`dynmatrix`] — Heap-allocated `DynMatrix<T>` with runtime dimensions
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!   (requires `alloc` feature, included with `std`). `Vec<T>` column-major storage
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!   (`col * nrows + row`). `from_rows()` accepts row-major data (transposes
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!   internally); `from_slice()` accepts column-major data directly.
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!   Implements [`MatrixRef`] / [`MatrixMut`], so all linalg free functions work
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!   automatically. [`DynVector<T>`] newtype for single-index vector access.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!   Includes `DynLu`, `DynCholesky`, `DynQr`, `DynSvd`, `DynSymmetricEigen`,
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!   `DynSchur` wrapper structs.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! - [`linalg`] — LU (partial pivoting), Cholesky (A = LL^H), QR (Householder),
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!   SVD (Householder bidiagonalization + Golub-Kahan implicit-shift QR),
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!   symmetric/Hermitian eigendecomposition (Householder tridiagonalization +
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!   implicit QR with Wilkinson shift), and real Schur decomposition (Hessenberg
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!   reduction + Francis double-shift QR). Each provides `solve()`, `inverse()`,
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!   `det()`, `eigenvalues()`, etc. Free functions operate on
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!   `&mut impl MatrixMut<T>` for in-place use; wrapper structs offer a
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!   higher-level API. Convenience methods on both `Matrix` and `DynMatrix`.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! - [`ode`] — Fixed-step RK4 and 7 adaptive Runge-Kutta solvers (RKF45,
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!   RKTS54, RKV65, RKV87, RKV98, RKV98NoInterp, RKV98Efficient). PI step-size
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!   controller with dense output / interpolation. Supports both vector and
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!   matrix state (e.g., state transition matrix propagation). RODAS4 L-stable
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!   Rosenbrock method for stiff systems (vector state, user-supplied or
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!   finite-difference Jacobians). Requires `ode` feature.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! - [`optim`] — Optimization: scalar root finding ([`optim::brent`],
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!   [`optim::newton_1d`]), BFGS quasi-Newton minimization ([`optim::minimize_bfgs`]),
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!   Gauss-Newton ([`optim::least_squares_gn`]) and Levenberg-Marquardt
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!   ([`optim::least_squares_lm`]) nonlinear least squares. Finite-difference
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!   Jacobian and gradient utilities. Fixed-size routines are no-alloc;
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!   dynamic-dimension counterparts ([`optim::minimize_bfgs_dyn`],
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!   [`optim::least_squares_gn_dyn`], [`optim::least_squares_lm_dyn`],
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!   [`optim::finite_difference_gradient_dyn`],
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!   [`optim::finite_difference_jacobian_dyn`]) operate on
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!   [`DynVector`] / [`DynMatrix`] and require the `alloc` feature.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!   Requires `optim` feature.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! - [`control`] — Digital IIR filters: [`control::Biquad`] second-order section and
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!   [`control::BiquadCascade`] for cascaded filters. Design functions for Butterworth
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!   and Chebyshev Type I lowpass/highpass. [`control::Pid`] discrete-time PID controller
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!   with anti-windup. [`control::lead_compensator`] and [`control::lag_compensator`] for
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!   compensator design via bilinear transform. PID tuning via [`control::FopdtModel`]
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!   (Ziegler-Nichols, Cohen-Coon, SIMC) and [`control::ziegler_nichols_ultimate`].
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!   No `complex` feature dependency. Requires `control` feature.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! - [`estimate`] — State estimation: [`estimate::Ekf`] (Extended Kalman Filter),
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!   [`estimate::Ukf`] (Unscented Kalman Filter), [`estimate::SrUkf`] (Square-Root UKF),
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!   [`estimate::Ckf`] (Cubature Kalman Filter), [`estimate::rts_smooth`] (RTS smoother),
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!   and [`estimate::BatchLsq`] (batch least-squares). Closure-based dynamics and
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!   measurement models, Joseph-form covariance update, Merwe-scaled sigma points.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!   EKF and BatchLsq are fully no-std; sigma-point filters and RTS require `alloc`.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!   Requires `estimate` feature.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! - [`interp`] — Interpolation: [`interp::LinearInterp`], [`interp::HermiteInterp`],
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!   [`interp::LagrangeInterp`] (barycentric), [`interp::CubicSpline`] (natural BCs),
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!   and [`interp::BilinearInterp`] (2D rectangular grid).
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!   Fixed-size (const N, stack-allocated, no-std) and dynamic variants (`Dyn*`, requires
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!   `alloc`). Out-of-bounds evaluations extrapolate. Requires `interp` feature.
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! - [`imageproc`] — 2D image processing on `DynMatrix` buffers. Full
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!   toolkit: convolution ([`imageproc::convolve2d`],
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!   [`imageproc::convolve2d_separable`]), blurs / sharpening / gradients /
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!   Laplacian / LoG, order-statistic filters (quickselect and
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!   Huang sliding-histogram for u16), morphology (Van Herk max/min plus
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!   opening / closing / top-hat / black-hat / morphology gradient),
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!   integral image and local mean / variance / stddev, thresholding
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!   (binary / Otsu / adaptive), Canny edge detection, Harris and
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!   Shi-Tomasi corners, difference of Gaussians and Gaussian pyramid,
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!   connected-components labeling (SAUF union-find, 4- or 8-connectivity,
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!   with per-component area / bbox / centroid / second moments, and
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!   optional `DynMatrix<u32>` or row-major `Vec<u32>` labels image),
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!   geometric utilities (flip, rotate 90°/180°/270°, pad, crop,
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!   resize bilinear and nearest). See [`imageproc`] module for details.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!   Requires `imageproc` feature (implies `alloc`).
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! - [`special`] — Special functions: [`special::gamma`], [`special::lgamma`],
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!   [`special::digamma`], [`special::beta`] / [`special::lbeta`],
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!   regularized incomplete gamma ([`special::gamma_inc`] / [`special::gamma_inc_upper`]),
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!   regularized incomplete beta ([`special::betainc`]),
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!   and error functions ([`special::erf`] / [`special::erfc`]).
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!   Generic over `FloatScalar` (f32/f64), fully no-std. Requires `special` feature.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! - [`quad`] — Numerical quadrature (integration): [`quad::gauss_legendre`] (N-point
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!   Gauss-Legendre, N=1..10,15,20), [`quad::adaptive_simpson`] (automatic subdivision),
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!   [`quad::trapezoid`] and [`quad::simpson`] (composite rules). All no-alloc.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!   Requires `quad` feature.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! - [`stats`] — Statistical distributions with [`stats::ContinuousDistribution`] and
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!   [`stats::DiscreteDistribution`] traits. Continuous: [`stats::Normal`],
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!   [`stats::Uniform`], [`stats::Exponential`], [`stats::Gamma`], [`stats::Beta`],
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!   [`stats::ChiSquared`], [`stats::StudentT`]. Discrete: [`stats::Bernoulli`],
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!   [`stats::Binomial`], [`stats::Poisson`]. Built-in [`stats::Rng`] (xoshiro256++)
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!   with `sample()` / `sample_array()` on every distribution.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!   Requires `stats` feature (implies `special`).
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! - [`quaternion`] — Unit quaternion for 3D rotations. Scalar-first `[w, x, y, z]`.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!   Construct from axis-angle, Euler angles, or rotation matrices. Supports
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!   Hamilton product, vector rotation, SLERP, and conversion back to matrices.
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! - [`traits`] — Element trait hierarchy:
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!   - [`Scalar`] — all matrix elements (`Copy + PartialEq + Debug + Zero + One + Num`)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!   - [`FloatScalar`] — real floats (`Scalar + Float`), used by quaternions
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!   - [`LinalgScalar`] — real floats and complex numbers, used by decompositions and norms
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!   - [`MatrixRef`] / [`MatrixMut`] — generic read/write access for algorithms
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! ## Complex matrices
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! Enable the `complex` feature to use decompositions with `Complex<f32>` /
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! `Complex<f64>`. Cholesky generalizes to Hermitian (A = LL^H), QR uses
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! complex Householder reflections, and norms return real values. Zero overhead
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! for real-only code paths.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! ## Cargo features
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! | Feature   | Default  | Description |
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! |-----------|----------|-------------|
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! | `std`     | yes      | Implies `alloc`. Hardware FPU via system libm |
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! | `alloc`   | via std  | `DynMatrix` / `DynVector` (heap-allocated, runtime-sized) |
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! | `ode`     | no       | ODE integration (RK4, adaptive solvers) |
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! | `optim`   | no       | Optimization (root finding, BFGS, Gauss-Newton, LM) |
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! | `control` | no       | Digital IIR filters, PID, lead/lag compensators, PID tuning |
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! | `estimate`| no       | State estimation (EKF, UKF). Implies `alloc` |
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! | `interp`  | no       | Interpolation (linear, Hermite, Lagrange, cubic spline, bilinear 2D) |
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! | `imageproc` | no     | 2D image processing: filters, morphology, integral image, thresholding, Canny, corners, DoG, pyramid, geometric. Implies `alloc` |
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! | `quad`    | no       | Numerical quadrature (Gauss-Legendre, adaptive Simpson, composite rules) |
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! | `special` | no       | Special functions (gamma, beta, erf, incomplete gamma/beta) |
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! | `stats`   | no       | Statistical distributions (Normal, Gamma, etc.) with sampling. Implies `special` |
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! | `libm`    | baseline | Pure-Rust software float fallback |
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! | `complex` | no       | `Complex<f32>` / `Complex<f64>` support via `num-complex` |
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! | `nalgebra`| no       | Conversions between numeris and nalgebra types |
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! | `serde`   | no       | Serialize/deserialize all types via serde |
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! | `rayon`   | no       | Multi-threaded parallelism on runtime-sized paths (e.g. dynamic finite-difference Jacobians, most `imageproc` filters). Implies `std` |
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! | `all`     | no       | All features |
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! ## Parallelism
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! SIMD is always-on and parallelizes *within* a core; the optional `rayon`
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! feature parallelizes *across* cores, and the two compose. It is opt-in
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! (rayon needs `std`, so it is never part of the no-std baseline) and purely
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! additive — builds without it are unchanged. Only heap-backed, runtime-sized
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! paths with independent, disjoint output columns are parallelized: dynamic
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! finite-difference Jacobians (the separate `_par` routines
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! [`optim::finite_difference_jacobian_dyn_par`],
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! [`optim::finite_difference_gradient_dyn_par`]) and most `imageproc` filters
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! (convolution/blur, rank & median, morphology, resize, local statistics).
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! Small fixed-size [`Matrix`] operations and order-sensitive reductions are
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! never parallelized. Each routine gates on total work (so small inputs stay
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! sequential) and writes to disjoint slices, so results are identical
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! regardless of thread count. Speedups run ~2.5–4× on large images.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! The feature is purely additive — it never changes an existing signature
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! (the parallel optim routines are *new* `_par` functions; the sequential ones
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! keep their `FnMut` bound).
[186](https://docs.rs#186)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
[188](https://docs.rs#188)// Coefficient tables (quadrature nodes/weights, Runge-Kutta tableaux, Lanczos
[189](https://docs.rs#189)// constants, …) are written at full published precision. The extra digits beyond
[190](https://docs.rs#190)// f64 are harmless (the compiler rounds to the nearest representable value), so
[191](https://docs.rs#191)// allow the lint crate-wide rather than truncating documented source values.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)#![allow(clippy::excessive_precision)]
[193](https://docs.rs#193)// Numerical code legitimately favors index-based loops: 2D access (`a[i][j]`,
[194](https://docs.rs#194)// `A[k][j]`), parallel indexing of several arrays by the same index, and
[195](https://docs.rs#195)// `f(i, j)` element constructors are clearer with explicit indices than with
[196](https://docs.rs#196)// zipped iterators. `needless_range_loop` is a known false positive here.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)#![allow(clippy::needless_range_loop)]
[198](https://docs.rs#198)// Iterative solvers (BFGS, Gauss-Newton, LM, …) keep evaluation counters
[199](https://docs.rs#199)// (`f_evals`, `j_evals`) that are *not* loop counters — they increment
[200](https://docs.rs#200)// conditionally / multiple times per iteration (line search, etc.), so they
[201](https://docs.rs#201)// cannot be replaced by `enumerate()`.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)#![allow(clippy::explicit_counter_loop)]
[203](https://docs.rs#203)// Low-level numeric kernels (SIMD matmul with strides, Van Herk passes, ODE
[204](https://docs.rs#204)// `integrate` entry points) genuinely need many parameters (dimensions, scratch
[205](https://docs.rs#205)// buffers, callbacks); factoring them into structs would only obscure the math.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)#![allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]
[207](https://docs.rs#207)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[209](https://docs.rs#209)#[cfg_attr(all(test, not(feature = "std")), macro_use)]
[210](https://docs.rs#210)extern crate alloc;
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)#[macro_use]
[213](https://docs.rs#213)mod macros;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)pub mod prelude;
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[217](https://docs.rs#217)pub mod dynmatrix;
[218](https://docs.rs#218)pub mod linalg;
[219](https://docs.rs#219)pub mod matrix;
[220](https://docs.rs#220)mod simd;
[221](https://docs.rs#221)// The `par` module backs the parallel paths: `imageproc` (always, sequential or
[222](https://docs.rs#222)// parallel) and the `optim` `_par` routines (only under `rayon`).
[223](https://docs.rs#223)#[cfg(any(
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    feature = "imageproc",
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    all(feature = "optim", feature = "alloc", feature = "rayon")
[226](https://docs.rs#226)))]
[227](https://docs.rs#227)mod par;
[228](https://docs.rs#228)// Marker trait used in public `imageproc` signatures; an implementation detail

[233](https://docs.rs#233)#[cfg(feature = "control")]
[234](https://docs.rs#234)pub mod control;
[235](https://docs.rs#235)#[cfg(feature = "estimate")]
[236](https://docs.rs#236)pub mod estimate;
[237](https://docs.rs#237)// Shared forward-difference Jacobian kernel for optim / estimate / ode.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)#[cfg(any(feature = "optim", feature = "estimate", feature = "ode"))]
[239](https://docs.rs#239)mod fdiff;
[240](https://docs.rs#240)#[cfg(feature = "imageproc")]
[241](https://docs.rs#241)pub mod imageproc;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)#[cfg(feature = "interp")]
[243](https://docs.rs#243)pub mod interp;
[244](https://docs.rs#244)#[cfg(feature = "nalgebra")]

# numeris::dynmatrix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/numeris/0.5.14/numeris/dynmatrix/index.html

[Skip to main content](#main-content)# Module dynmatrix

[Source](../../src/numeris/dynmatrix/mod.rs.html#1-523) - `pub use `- [aliases](aliases/index.html)::*;

- [aliases](aliases/index.html)
- Pre-defined type aliases for common `DynMatrix`and`DynVector`element types.

- [DimensionMismatch](struct.DimensionMismatch.html)
- Dimension mismatch error for fallible conversions.
- [DynCholesky](struct.DynCholesky.html)
- Cholesky decomposition of a dynamically-sized (Hermitian) positive-definite matrix.
- [DynLu](struct.DynLu.html)
- LU decomposition of a dynamically-sized square matrix.
- [DynMatrix](struct.DynMatrix.html)
- Dynamically-sized heap-allocated matrix.
- [DynQr](struct.DynQr.html)
- QR decomposition of a dynamically-sized matrix (M >= N).
- [DynQrPivot](struct.DynQrPivot.html)
- Rank-revealing QR decomposition with column pivoting for dynamically-sized matrices.
- [DynSchur](struct.DynSchur.html)
- Real Schur decomposition of a dynamically-sized square matrix.
- [DynSvd](struct.DynSvd.html)
- Singular value decomposition of a dynamically-sized matrix.
- [DynSymmetricEigen](struct.DynSymmetricEigen.html)
- Symmetric/Hermitian eigendecomposition of a dynamically-sized square matrix.
- [DynVector](struct.DynVector.html)
- Dynamically-sized column vector (wraps an N×1 `DynMatrix`).

[nrows](https://docs.rs#tymethod.nrows)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html);
[ncols](https://docs.rs#tymethod.ncols)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html);
[get](https://docs.rs#tymethod.get)(&self, row: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), col: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html);
[col_as_slice](https://docs.rs#tymethod.col_as_slice)(&self, col: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), row_start: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html);
}## Expand description

Read-only access to a matrix-like type.

This trait allows algorithms to operate generically over
both fixed-size `Matrix` and future `DynMatrix` types.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use numeris::{Matrix, MatrixRef};
fn trace<T: numeris::Scalar>(m: &impl MatrixRef<T>) -> T {
    let mut sum = T::zero();
    let n = m.nrows().min(m.ncols());
    for i in 0..n {
        sum = sum + *m.get(i, i);
    }
    sum
}
let m = Matrix::new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]);
assert_eq!(trace(&m), 5.0);
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/numeris/traits.rs.html#166)#### fn [col_as_slice](https://docs.rs#tymethod.col_as_slice)(&self, col: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), row_start: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/numeris/traits.rs.html#166)

#### fn [col_as_slice](https://docs.rs#tymethod.col_as_slice)(&self, col: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), row_start: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)

Contiguous slice of column `col` from row `row_start` to end.

Returns `&[T]` of length `nrows - row_start`. Available because
both `Matrix` and `DynMatrix` use column-major contiguous storage.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

- Cholesky decomposition of a fixed-size (Hermitian) positive-definite matrix.
- [LuDecomposition](struct.LuDecomposition.html)
- LU decomposition of a fixed-size square matrix.
- [QrDecomposition](struct.QrDecomposition.html)
- QR decomposition of a fixed-size matrix (M >= N).
- [QrPivotDecomposition](struct.QrPivotDecomposition.html)
- Rank-revealing QR decomposition with column pivoting.
- [SchurDecomposition](struct.SchurDecomposition.html)
- Real Schur decomposition of a fixed-size square matrix.
- [SvdDecomposition](struct.SvdDecomposition.html)
- Singular value decomposition of a fixed-size matrix (M ≥ N).

- [LinalgError](enum.LinalgError.html)

- [cholesky_rank1_downdate](fn.cholesky_rank1_downdate.html)
- Rank-1 downdate: given lower-triangular `L`where`A = L·Lᵀ`, compute`L'`in-place such that`A - v·vᵀ = L'·L'ᵀ`.
- [cholesky_rank1_update](fn.cholesky_rank1_update.html)
- Rank-1 update: given lower-triangular `L`where`A = L·Lᵀ`, compute`L'`in-place such that`A + v·vᵀ = L'·L'ᵀ`.
- [expm](fn.expm.html)
- Matrix exponential via scaling-and-squaring with [13,13] Padé approximation.
